## Where the Framing Breaks Down

**The X-55's central quantity has no instrument.** This is the second article in this series whose binding number is an estimate rather than a reading, after a vehicle whose entire argument turned on a launch price \[[X-Planes: Orbital Sciences X-34][related_post_a331_orbital_sciences_x34]\].

**A flying demonstrator can settle several things and cannot settle the one it was named for.** It can settle whether a bonded composite fuselage with skins twenty metres long will carry flight loads, whether it can be built at all, whether the tooling closes, and whether the structure behaves as predicted once instrumented. **It cannot settle a recurring cost**, because a recurring cost is a property of a production run and the demonstrator is a run of one.

**What it can do is retire a manufacturing risk, and that is a real thing to retire.** Before June 2009 the proposition that a fuselage of this size could be laid up, bonded, closed and flown without an autoclave was an assertion, and afterwards it was not \[[The Carbon Comet, Lockheed Martin][ref_carbon_comet]\].

**But a manufacturing risk is not the whole of the technical risk, as the fastener giveback shows.** The certification of a bonded unitised primary structure was an open problem before the X-55 flew and remained one long afterwards \[[Market Trends, the Composites Affordability Initiative, Part I, CompositesWorld][ref_cw_cai]\] \[[Clay et al. 2021][research_failsafe_intro]\], and **no single flying article could have closed it**, because what a certification basis wants is not a demonstration but a body of evidence about how the structure fails.

**The registry entry claims more than a demonstrator can deliver**, and the gap between the two is the subject of this article.

## The Source Base

**The research survey holds 4,803 records, and every one of them is cited in the survey in the section headed The Contemporary Literature.**
They are drawn from NASA's Technical Reports Server, the Defense Technical Information Center and the
journal literature indexed by Crossref. The reference list holds 4,909 definitions in total, being the
research records together with forty-four reference sources, seven books and fifty-five links to earlier
articles in this series.

### The Definition of Primary

**Primacy is a property of the document, and this survey derives it from the identifier.** A research
record is a report primary when its address is on the NASA Technical Reports Server or its digital
object identifier carries the 10.21236 prefix under which Crossref registers Defense Technical
Information Center reports.

**284 of the 4,803 research records are report primaries, being
5.9 percent**, counted by that rule.
**197 of those are defence-registry reports and 87 are report-server
documents**, which is the reverse of the balance in the previous article in this series and is
simply a fact about who paid. **Sonic boom research was a civil agency's and this was the Air
Force's.**

**A report share of 5.9 percent is small, and it is a fact about who did the work.**
**Composite manufacturing was done by contractors, and a contractor's process hours, cure schedules and
scrap rates are a competitive asset rather than a publication.** What the registries do hold is the
government's own share of the work, which is the certification question and the predecessor programmes.

**Both kinds of primary are reported, because the measure cannot see most of this article's.** The
article names and argues from **29 primary documents**, and
**23 of them carry no identifier the corpus measure recognises**. The
designation registry \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum, MDS Designators Allocated After 19 August 1998][ref_mds_addendum]\], the material datasheet \[[MTM45-1 Prepreg Technical Data Sheet, Cytec Industrial
Materials][ref_mtm45_datasheet]\], the manufacturer's own account of the build \[[The Carbon Comet,
Lockheed Martin][ref_carbon_comet]\] and the programme's own conference papers \[[Butler 2000][research_cai_butler]\] are every one of them primary, and every one is
invisible to a count that looks for a report-server prefix. **The fraction and the count are reported side by side
and the measure is not adjusted to flatter either.**

**The report primaries remain a generation older than the survey.** Their median year is
1993 against 2011 for the corpus, a gap of
18 years.

### The Age of the Literature

**4,421 of the research records carry a year at or before this article's
own dateline, and their median is 2011**, with the range running from
1927 to 2025. Publication rate by decade, in records a year, is
set out below. The 2020s are counted over six years rather than ten, so the figures are rates
and not counts.

**A further 148 records carry a later year and are excluded from every
statistic in this section**, being 3.1 percent of the corpus. They remain
in the reference list, which cites later work as well as earlier. **A statistic is a different thing
from a citation.** A rate computed over papers that had not been written when this article is dated
would be a claim about the future wearing the clothes of a measurement.
**A further 234 records carry no year at all**, and some fraction of those is
certainly later than the dateline too, which no filter can reach.

| Decade | Records a year |
|---|---|
| 1950s | 0.8 |
| 1960s | 3.9 |
| 1970s | 12.9 |
| 1980s | 35.9 |
| 1990s | 74.8 |
| 2000s | 77.8 |
| 2010s | 126.6 |
| 2020s | 182.0 |

**This literature has grown in every decade since the 1950s and has never once contracted**,
which is worth setting beside the previous article in this series. **The sonic boom corpus
fell by more than forty percent through the 1980s**, in the decade after the American supersonic
transport was cancelled and overland supersonic flight was prohibited. **Composite
manufacturing was never prohibited and its curve shows it.** A literature records what was
permitted as faithfully as it records what was discovered.

### Thin Subjects

**Seven subjects that this article's derivations depend on have thin literatures.** Each count below is
the number of research records in this survey whose title carries at least one of the listed terms,
with a hyphen read as a space. Where a row joins two groups of terms with the word together, a title
must carry a term from each group.

| Subject | Title terms counted | Records |
|---|---|---|
| the elevation of the shop floor and the vacuum it allows | altitude, elevation, barometric, ambient pressure, atmospheric pressure together with vacuum bag, vacuum bagging, out of autoclave, vacuum bag only, consolidation, prepreg, debulk, debulking, compaction | 0 |
| the surface tension that holds a small void open | surface tension, capillary pressure, laplace pressure, interfacial tension | 3 |
| the DiBenedetto relation behind the vitrification ceiling | dibenedetto, di benedetto | 0 |
| the time to install a fastener | fastener, fasteners, rivet, rivets, riveting together with installation, install, installing, touch time, assembly time, labour, labor, hours, cost, costs | 6 |
| fasteners as disbond arrest in a bonded structure | fastener, fasteners, bolt, bolts, rivet, rivets together with disbond, delamination arrest, crack arrest, fail safe, arrest | 4 |
| the X-55 and the Advanced Composite Cargo Aircraft | x 55, x55, x 55a, advanced composite cargo aircraft | 2 |
| the out-life of a prepreg | out life, out time, outlife, outtime, tack life, working life, shelf life, storage life, prepreg ageing, prepreg aging, room temperature ageing, room temperature aging, ambient temperature storable | 12 |

**No title in the survey ties consolidation to the elevation of the shop floor.** The result that a
vacuum bag at Air Force Plant 42 can apply only 13.39 pounds per square inch, and that the datasheet's
gauge vacuum is unattainable there, therefore stands on the standard atmosphere and the datasheet alone.

**The capillary literature is about filling, not about closing voids.** All three titles that name surface tension
or capillary pressure concern the impregnation of a dry preform, so the radius below which a bag
cannot close a void rests on the Laplace relation and an assumed surface tension rather than on a
measured one.

**Vitrification is well studied and the relation this article inverts is not named once.**
Vitrification appears in 28 titles and none of them names the DiBenedetto relation, two of whose
three parameters are taken here as assumptions because neither is published for this resin.

**The labour a fastener costs has almost no literature in this survey.** Six titles name the installation of a fastener,
and every one of them concerns the equipment, the automation or the ergonomics of installation and none names the time
or the cost per fastener, so the
touch times in the fastener arithmetic are the article's assumptions and are stated as a range.

**The fastener given back to a bonded structure has a small and specific literature.** Four titles name
fasteners as a disbond or delamination arrest, and two of them are the ones the subsection headed Some of the
Fasteners Come Back cites.

**The designation itself is not a research subject.** Two titles name the Advanced Composite
Cargo Aircraft and none names the X-55, so the claim in this article's closing sentence rests on two
dates in the register and not on any body of research.

**Out-life is the constraint this article argues binds the whole method, and its literature is
12 titles under several names**, being out-time, ageing, working life, storage life and
ambient storability.

**The documents the argument rests on are identified by the programme's own citation chain and not by the survey.** Following the Composites Affordability Initiative and the certification literature it leads to gives the papers the programme's own engineers treated as the point. A survey cannot do that, because its admission rule decides whether a record belongs to a subject and not which record carries the argument. **The survey says what exists, and the citation chain says which of the 4,803 records the argument needs.**

### What the Survey Admits

**A record is admitted only when a person reading its title finds it on this article's subject**, the subject being the composite airframe and its qualification, bonding, thermoset cure, placement and out-life, manufacturing cost, inspection, out-of-autoclave consolidation, voids, tooling and distortion, the laminate as a material, drilling and fastening, the aeroplane, and the standard atmosphere. The atmosphere is admitted for one reason, which is that the consolidation pressure computation above needs it. **The residual admits a title on a fibre-reinforced composite as a material when it names none of those subjects**, being a general account of the material family, the fibre and its surface, or a functional property such as conduction, shielding, fire or ablation.

**Two adjacent literatures are excluded deliberately.** Wind turbine blade manufacture is the largest infused composite structure anybody builds and shares most of this article's process vocabulary. Marine composites share the rest. **Both are adjacent rather than contaminating**, and both are left out because the subject is an airframe, which means the count in the survey in the section headed The Contemporary Literature is smaller than the technology's full literature and is not offered as that. **The cost and schedule literature of defence acquisition is excluded for the same reason**, so the claim that the programme was built cheaper and slower stands on two published dates rather than on the survey. Civil engineering is excluded as well, including fibre-reinforced polymer bonded to concrete, masonry, timber or steel to strengthen a building or a bridge, and so are pipes and risers, and the structural design of cars, boats, wheels, gears and sports goods.

**Many words this subject depends on also name something else, and a record that shares only such a word is excluded.** Nondestructive inspection shares an abbreviation with dam safety inspection. Entrapped air and the name Darcy also belong to hydraulic, soil and petroleum reservoir studies, and consolidation also names the settlement of soils and dredged slurry. Ultrasonic attenuation is also studied in metals and superconductors, and chemical reactors and hydrometallurgy have autoclaves of their own. Adhesive bonding also names timber and wood-panel construction and the die attach of electronics, shimming also names the shimming of magnets for magnetic resonance imaging, and a void also names the diffusion and casting voids of metallurgy. The glass transition is also a property of every amorphous polymer, rubber and inorganic glass, and cure also names the vulcanisation of rubber. Restorative dentistry uses bond strength, cure kinetics, resin composite and degree of conversion as its own terms of art, the textile and paper industries have their own standards for conditioning atmospheres, and a short learning curve is an idiom. A cost model or a design-for-assembly study of an unrelated product, such as a solar cell, a circuit board or a kitchen appliance, and the operating and maintenance cost of aircraft, are excluded because the argument prices manufacture and assembly.

**Editorial notices are excluded, because a notice is not a research work.** That is every record whose title opens with Correction, Erratum, Errata, Corrigendum, Withdrawn, Withdrawal or Retraction, or whose identifier carries the numbered notice suffix, such as .c1, that the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics gives a correction, and every record whose title declares itself a withdrawal notice. A title that names a correction as its technical method, such as a correction response surface design, is a research work and is kept. A book's preface or other front matter, a review of a book, a reference or definition entry of two pages or fewer, a table of standard values of two pages or fewer printed as a textbook appendix, a journal's listing of a newly issued publication, the resolution of a standards conference and a second deposit of a document already in the survey are not admitted either, while an authored encyclopedia article of more than two pages and a textbook chapter are research works and are kept.

**Some records of doubtful relevance are kept.** Thermoset cure and warpage in microelectronic packages are kept as thermoset cure, and so are epoxy cure kinetics for art restoration and the low-temperature cure of powder coatings, because the chemistry is the subject. Learning-curve and cost-method titles that name no product are kept as cost-method literature. Process studies whose part is a car body, a boat or an offshore structure are kept as process literature, because the process is the subject. Each shares a method with this subject rather than only a word, and a reader may weigh it accordingly.

**Every research title has been read for relevance, so the off-topic share that remains is a matter of reading judgement.** A reading of titles cannot show that a work is relevant in substance, so this is a statement about titles only.

## Epistemic State

**What is documented.** The registry entry, the donor airframe, the structural arrangement, the material family, the part and fastener counts, the contract value, the required and achieved first flight dates, the cause of the delay, and the aeroplane's disposition.

**What is computed here and stated as such.** The pressure at Plant 42 and the consolidation pressures that follow from it. The pressure vessel scaling. The Boyle's law void arithmetic and the surface-tension threshold beneath it. The activation energy fitted to the datasheet, and the dwell comparison built on it. The vitrification ceiling. The Darcy transport times. The convective scaling. The fastener labour and the break-even run. The layup rate implied by the out-life and the ply ceiling implied by that. **None of those is a measurement of this aeroplane.** They are what the published constants imply, and where an assumption drives an answer the assumption is named beside it.

**Four assumptions carry more weight than the rest and are collected here.** The surface tension of the uncured resin is taken at 0.035 newtons per metre, a representative value and not a measurement of this material. The Kozeny constant, the fibre volume fraction and the two viscosities in the transport calculation are representative in the same way, and the transport conclusion survives a hundredfold error in the permeability because the length goes as its square root. **Two of the three DiBenedetto parameters are assumptions**, and the vitrification ceiling moves between 0.741 and 0.899 across the range they plausibly occupy, while the conclusion drawn from them does not move at all. **The minutes and the burdened rate in the fastener arithmetic are assumptions spanning a factor of ten**, and the break-even run spans the same factor in consequence.

**What is uncertain.** The ninety against ninety-eight percent fastener discrepancy is unresolved. **The trade press calls the fuselage sixty feet long in one account and its skins sixty-five feet long in another, and the encyclopaedia entry gives fifty-five feet for the fuselage with the nose attached** \[[Out-of-Autoclave Prepregs, Hype or Revolution, CompositesWorld][ref_cw_ooa]\] \[[Advanced Composite Cargo Aircraft Proves Large Structure Practicality, CompositesWorld][ref_cw_acca]\] \[[Lockheed Martin X-55][ref_x55_wikipedia]\]. This article uses the skin length throughout, which makes the skin area and every rate derived from it an upper estimate. The number of flights was expected in advance to be 15 to 20, and no primary record of the total has come to light. The cure schedule used on the fuselage is not published, and the trade press reports an oven cure at 177 degrees, 350 Fahrenheit, with vacuum pressure \[[Advanced Composite Cargo Aircraft Proves Large Structure Practicality, CompositesWorld][ref_cw_acca]\], where the datasheet's vacuum bag cure is 120 degrees with a post-cure at 180, which is most likely a description of the post-cure rather than a contradiction. **The article does not assume which.**

**What could not be verified.** No Air Force Research Laboratory final report on this programme was located in the public report registries, and the absence is reported rather than treated as evidence of absence. **The number of arrest fasteners a certification basis would demand of a structure like this one is not published and is not estimated here.** **The claim that the bond failure was caused by out-life is not made**, because no source states it. The out-life argument here is a mechanism the literature supports and not a diagnosis of this event.

**What the corpus excludes.** 148 records carry a year later than this article's dateline and are excluded from every statistic while remaining in the reference list. A further 234 carry no year at all and cannot be filtered either way.

## Out of Scope

The aerodynamics of the aeroplane, which were the Dornier's and were not modified. The flight test instrumentation and the loads it measured, for which no public dataset was found. Thermoplastic composites, which answer the same question a different way and would double the article. The certification of bonded primary structure, which is named because the survey covers it and is not argued here. **And the aeroplane's contribution to any later programme, information a contractor does not publish.**

## Conclusion

**The X-55 was given a number to validate that an airframe could be built faster and cheaper, and the record shows it was built cheaper and slower.**

**The two halves of the registry entry were never symmetric.** The cost claim is a comparison against an estimate of an aeroplane nobody built. The schedule claim is a comparison against a date, and the date was missed by seven to nine months, by source, because the skin on the lower fuselage did not bond and a second fuselage had to be made. **The demonstration was delayed by the thing being demonstrated.**

**The arithmetic shows that this should have been expected, and why.** Low-temperature curing costs three times the oven dwell of the cure it replaces, so the time saving cannot come from the chemistry. It has to come from part count, and part count is a recurring saving that a run of one cannot collect. **Meanwhile the same technology that lets a part be large enough to be worth unitising puts a chemical clock on how long its layup may take**, and a programme built on the case for fewer and larger parts still assembled its fuselage from eight of them.

**Nor is the part-count saving wholly the programme's to keep.** Certifying a bonded primary structure has meant putting mechanical fasteners back through the bondline as a second load path and a disbond arrest, and those take back some of what unitisation removed while giving up the stiffness and the fatigue performance that motivated bonding. **How much is given back is not published and this article does not guess.**

**None of that makes the aeroplane a failure.** It flew, it carried its loads, and it did so on a cooperative agreement of 49,097,981 dollars for its design and build. **It retired a manufacturing risk.** A bonded composite fuselage with skins 19.8 metres long could be built outside an autoclave, tooled, closed and flown, and before June 2009 that was an assertion.

**What it did not retire, and could not have, is the certification risk.** An Air Force Research Laboratory programme was still publishing on fail-safe features for bonded unitised structure in 2023, fourteen years later, **so the question of whether such a structure can be certified without putting the fasteners back was open before the X-55 flew and remained open long after.**

**And what it could not do was measure the quantity in its own mission statement**, because that quantity only exists across a production run. **The arithmetic puts that run at between forty and four hundred aeroplanes and at about a hundred on the middle assumption**, and there was never going to be a second.

**One number in this article deserves to be kept for its own sake.** The pressure a vacuum bag can apply is the pressure of the air outside it, so the consolidation available to an out-of-autoclave process at Air Force Plant 42 is 13.39 pounds per square inch against the 14.7 of sea level, and the material datasheet asks for a vacuum the site's entire atmosphere cannot supply. **A manufacturing specification for an aeroplane turns out to depend on the elevation of the floor it is built on.**

**The number arrived 139 days after the first flight, which is the right order for a designation that was recognising a result rather than authorising an attempt.**

## Equations

<!-- Equations generated by _lib/equations.py from _sources/equations/. Edit the data file and regenerate. Do not edit this section by hand. -->

This section collects the 38 display equations of the article in the order they appear,
each under its number and reproduced exactly as it stands in the text.
A title in bold names an established result,
and a title in italics beginning with the word Bespoke names a construction made for this analysis.
Of the 38, 28 are established and 10 are bespoke.
Consolidation pressures are in pounds per square inch, cure dwells in hours, temperatures in kelvin in the Arrhenius relations but in degrees Celsius in the glass transition relations, where only differences enter, and lengths and areas in metres, while several letters are reused, so $D$ is the sandwich bending stiffness and then the fuselage diameter, $L$ a vessel, flow path, laminate or skin length, $H$ the scale height and $H(t)$ the reaction heat released, $h$ an altitude, a heat transfer coefficient or working hours a day, $\alpha$ the degree of cure and $\alpha_{\text{th}}$ a thermal diffusivity, and $R$ the molar gas constant while $R_{\text{air}}$ is the specific gas constant of air.

**Equation 1, Bending Stiffness of a Sandwich Panel.**
A sandwich takes its bending stiffness almost wholly from two facesheets held apart by the core, approximately half the facesheet modulus times the facesheet thickness times the square of the core depth.

$$
D \approx \frac{E_{f}\,t_{\text{face}}\,h_{c}^{2}}{2}
\tag{1}
$$

**Equation 2, Thin-Walled Pressure Vessel Wall Thickness.**
Hoop stress fixes the wall thickness of a cylindrical vessel as the pressure times the radius over the allowable stress.
[Pressure Vessel][ref_pressure_vessel]

$$
t_{w} = \frac{p\,r}{\sigma_{\text{allow}}}
\tag{2}
$$

**Equation 3, Shell Mass of a Cylindrical Pressure Vessel.**
The shell mass is the density times the shell area times the wall thickness, so it rises with the square of the radius times the length.
[Pressure Vessel][ref_pressure_vessel]

$$
m_{\text{shell}} = 2 \pi \rho \, r \, L \, t_{w} = \frac{2 \pi \rho \, p \, r^{2} L}{\sigma_{\text{allow}}}
\tag{3}
$$

**Equation 4, Consolidation Pressure Under a Bag and in an Autoclave.**
A vacuum bag consolidates with the ambient pressure less the pressure inside the bag, and an autoclave adds its gauge pressure to that differential.
[Vacuum Bag Moulding][ref_vacuum_bagging]

$$
\Delta p_{\text{bag}} = p_{\text{amb}} - p_{\text{in}}
\qquad\qquad
\Delta p_{\text{autoclave}} = p_{\text{gauge}} + p_{\text{amb}} - p_{\text{in}}
\tag{4}
$$

**Equation 5, Ratio of Autoclave to Vacuum Bag Consolidation Pressure.**
With the bag fully evacuated the ratio of autoclave to bag consolidation pressure is one plus the gauge pressure over the ambient pressure.

$$
\frac{\Delta p_{\text{autoclave}}}{\Delta p_{\text{bag}}} = 1 + \frac{p_{\text{gauge}}}{p_{\text{amb}}}
\tag{5}
$$

**Equation 6, Pressure in the Standard Troposphere.**
The standard atmosphere gives the ambient pressure below the tropopause as a power of the linearly falling temperature ratio.
[U.S. Standard Atmosphere][ref_us_standard_atmosphere]
[Barometric Formula][ref_barometric]

$$
p(h) = p_{0}\left(1 - \frac{\lambda h}{T_{0}}\right)^{\frac{g}{R_{\text{air}}\lambda}}
\tag{6}
$$

**Equation 7, Sea-Level Pressure Gradient and Scale Height.**
Differentiating the hydrostatic balance at sea level gives a pressure gradient equal to the sea-level pressure over the scale height.

$$
\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}p}{\mathrm{d}h}\right|_{0} = -\frac{p_{0}\,g}{R_{\text{air}} T_{0}} = -\frac{p_{0}}{H}
\qquad\qquad
H = \frac{R_{\text{air}} T_{0}}{g}
\tag{7}
$$

**Equation 8, Boyle's Law for an Entrapped Gas.**
At constant temperature the volume of an entrapped gas is inversely proportional to its pressure.
[Boyle's Law][ref_boyle]

$$
V_{1} = V_{0}\,\frac{p_{0}}{p_{1}}
\tag{8}
$$

**Equation 9, Void Fraction After Isothermal Compression.**
With the solid taken as incompressible beside the gas, compressing the voids by Boyle's law changes the void fraction as the compressed void volume over the new total volume.
[Boyle's Law][ref_boyle]

$$
\phi_{1} = \frac{\phi_{0}\,p_{0}/p_{1}}{\left(1-\phi_{0}\right) + \phi_{0}\,p_{0}/p_{1}}
\tag{9}
$$

**Equation 10, Pressure Ratio Required for a Target Void Fraction.**
Inverting the void fraction relation gives the pressure ratio that a specified final void fraction demands.

$$
\frac{p_{1}}{p_{0}} = \frac{\phi_{0}}{\phi_{1}}\cdot\frac{1-\phi_{1}}{1-\phi_{0}}
\tag{10}
$$

**Equation 11, Laplace Pressure of a Void.**
The gas in a spherical void exceeds the resin pressure by twice the surface tension over the void radius.
[Laplace Pressure][ref_laplace_pressure]

$$
p_{\text{void}} - p_{\text{resin}} = \frac{2\gamma}{r}
\tag{11}
$$

**Equation 12, Smallest Void Radius Closed by a Given Pressure.**
Setting the Laplace excess equal to the available consolidation pressure gives the radius below which pressure cannot close a void.
[Laplace Pressure][ref_laplace_pressure]

$$
r_{\text{min}} = \frac{2\gamma}{\Delta p}
\tag{12}
$$

**Equation 13, Henry's Law.**
The concentration of gas dissolved in the resin is proportional to the pressure applied.
[Henry's Law][ref_henry]

$$
c = k_{H}\,p
\tag{13}
$$

**Equation 14, Darcy's Law.**
The volumetric flux through a porous medium is the permeability over the viscosity times the pressure gradient.
[Darcy's Law][ref_darcy]

$$
q = -\frac{k}{\mu}\,\nabla p
\tag{14}
$$

**Equation 15, Kozeny-Carman Permeability of a Fibre Bed.**
The Kozeny-Carman relation sets the permeability of a fibre bed by the square of the fibre diameter and the cube of the open fraction over the square of the fibre volume fraction and the Kozeny constant.

$$
k = \frac{d_{f}^{2}\,\left(1 - V_{f}\right)^{3}}{\kappa\,V_{f}^{2}}
\tag{15}
$$

*Equation 16, Bespoke Sweep Time Through a Dry Tow Network.*
The article takes a linear pressure gradient over the path to estimate the time a fluid needs to sweep the channel network as viscosity times porosity times the square of the path length over permeability times pressure difference.

$$
t_{\text{sweep}} = \frac{\mu\,\varphi\,L^{2}}{k\,\Delta p}
\tag{16}
$$

**Equation 17, Ratio of Resin to Air Sweep Times.**
For the same path, permeability and pressure difference the two sweep times stand in the ratio of the two viscosities.

$$
\frac{t_{\text{resin}}}{t_{\text{air}}} = \frac{\mu_{\text{resin}}}{\mu_{\text{air}}}
\tag{17}
$$

**Equation 18, Degree of Cure.**
The degree of cure is the reaction heat released so far as a fraction of the ultimate heat of reaction, as a calorimeter reports it.
[Thermosetting Polymer][ref_thermosetting]

$$
\alpha(t) = \frac{H(t)}{H_{\text{ult}}}
\tag{18}
$$

**Equation 19, Autocatalytic Cure Rate Model.**
The two-constant autocatalytic model fits epoxy amine cure with a rate that rises from zero before it falls.
[Vyazovkin and Sbirrazzuoli 1996][research_vyazovkin_sbirrazzuoli_1996]
[Keenan 1987][research_keenan_1987]

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}\alpha}{\mathrm{d}t} = \left(k_{1} + k_{2}\,\alpha^{m}\right)\left(1 - \alpha\right)^{n}
\tag{19}
$$

**Equation 20, Arrhenius Dependence of Cure Time on Temperature.**
Because both rate constants follow an Arrhenius law, the time to reach a given degree of cure rises exponentially as the temperature falls.
[Arrhenius Equation][ref_arrhenius]
[Kratz et al. 2012][research_kratz_thermal_models]

$$
t \;=\; A_{0} \exp\!\left(\frac{E_{a}}{R\,T}\right)
\tag{20}
$$

**Equation 21, Activation Energy From Two Isothermal Dwells.**
Two dwells at two temperatures that reach the same state fix an activation energy through the logarithm of their ratio over the difference of reciprocal temperatures.
[Arrhenius Equation][ref_arrhenius]

$$
E_{a} \;=\; R\,\frac{\ln\!\left(t_{1}/t_{2}\right)}{1/T_{1} - 1/T_{2}}
\tag{21}
$$

*Equation 22, Bespoke Apparent Activation Energy From the Datasheet Cures.*
The datasheet's twenty hours at 80 degrees Celsius and two hours at 130 are treated as reaching a common state, an assumption the article adopts although the cures are not iso-conversional, giving an apparent activation energy of about 54.5 kilojoules per mole.
[MTM45-1 Prepreg Technical Data Sheet, Cytec Industrial Materials][ref_mtm45_datasheet]

$$
E_{a} = 8.314 \times \frac{\ln\left(20/2\right)}{1/353.15 - 1/403.15} = \frac{19.14}{3.512 \times 10^{-4}} \approx 54{,}510
\tag{22}
$$

**Equation 23, Arrhenius Ratio of Dwell Times.**
The ratio of dwell times at two temperatures is the exponential of the activation energy over the gas constant times the difference of reciprocal temperatures.

$$
\frac{t_{\text{lo}}}{t_{\text{hi}}} = \exp\!\left[\frac{E_{a}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_{\text{lo}}} - \frac{1}{T_{\text{hi}}}\right)\right]
\tag{23}
$$

*Equation 24, Bespoke Predicted Dwell at 120 Degrees and the Datasheet Margin.*
Extrapolating from two hours at 130 degrees with the fitted apparent activation energy predicts about three hours at 120, so the datasheet's four hours carries a margin of about 32 percent.
[MTM45-1 Prepreg Technical Data Sheet, Cytec Industrial Materials][ref_mtm45_datasheet]

$$
t_{\text{lo}} = 2 \exp\left[6{,}556 \left(\frac{1}{393.15} - \frac{1}{403.15}\right)\right] \approx 3.025,
\qquad
\frac{4}{3.025} - 1 \approx 0.322
\tag{24}
$$

**Equation 25, Fourier Conduction Time of a Laminate.**
The time for heat to equilibrate across a laminate is the square of its thickness over its through-thickness diffusivity.

$$
\tau = \frac{L^{2}}{\alpha_{\text{th}}}
\tag{25}
$$

*Equation 26, Bespoke Conduction Time of a Six Millimetre Laminate.*
At a through-thickness diffusivity of three ten-millionths of a square metre per second, a representative value the article assumes, a six millimetre laminate equilibrates in two minutes, under one percent of the four hour dwell.
[Thermal Diffusivity][ref_thermal_diffusivity]

$$
\tau = \frac{\left(6 \times 10^{-3}\right)^{2}}{3 \times 10^{-7}} = 120,
\qquad
\frac{\tau}{t} = \frac{120}{14{,}400} \approx 0.0083
\tag{26}
$$

*Equation 27, Bespoke Pressure Scaling of the Convective Coefficient.*
The Dittus-Boelter form makes the convective coefficient scale as the 0.8 power of gas pressure once the article holds velocity, temperature and geometry equal between the oven and the autoclave.
[Nusselt Number][ref_nusselt]

$$
\mathrm{Nu} = C_{Nu}\,\mathrm{Re}^{0.8}\,\mathrm{Pr}^{1/3}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\frac{h_{\text{autoclave}}}{h_{\text{oven}}} \sim \left(\frac{p_{\text{autoclave}}}{p_{\text{oven}}}\right)^{0.8}
\tag{27}
$$

*Equation 28, Bespoke Convective Advantage of the Autoclave.*
At the consolidation pressure ratio of 7.35 the coefficient rises by about 4.93, or by 3.31 at an exponent of 0.6 that the article assumes as the lower end of the range.

$$
\frac{h_{\text{autoclave}}}{h_{\text{oven}}} \sim 7.35^{0.8} \approx 4.93,
\qquad
7.35^{0.6} \approx 3.31
\tag{28}
$$

**Equation 29, DiBenedetto Relation.**
The DiBenedetto relation gives the rise of the glass transition temperature with degree of cure between its uncured and fully cured values.
[Glass Transition][ref_glass_transition]

$$
\frac{T_{g} - T_{g0}}{T_{g\infty} - T_{g0}} = \frac{\lambda_{D}\,\alpha}{1 - \left(1 - \lambda_{D}\right)\alpha}
\tag{29}
$$

**Equation 30, Vitrification Limit on the Degree of Cure.**
Setting the glass transition equal to the cure temperature and inverting the DiBenedetto relation gives the conversion at which the resin vitrifies.

$$
\alpha_{\text{vit}} = \frac{f}{\lambda_{D} + \left(1 - \lambda_{D}\right) f}
\qquad\qquad
f = \frac{T_{\text{cure}} - T_{g0}}{T_{g\infty} - T_{g0}}
\tag{30}
$$

*Equation 31, Bespoke Vitrification Ceilings at 120 and 160 Degrees.*
With the datasheet's fully cured glass transition of 180 degrees and an uncured value of minus 20 degrees and a curvature parameter of 0.5 that the article assumes, a 120 degree cure stops near 0.824 and the wet glass transition of 160 degrees demands 0.947.
[MTM45-1 Prepreg Technical Data Sheet, Cytec Industrial Materials][ref_mtm45_datasheet]

$$
f = \frac{120 - \left(-20\right)}{180 - \left(-20\right)} = 0.70,
\qquad
\alpha_{\text{vit}} = \frac{0.70}{0.5 + 0.5 \times 0.70} \approx 0.824,
\qquad
\frac{0.90}{0.5 + 0.5 \times 0.90} \approx 0.947
\tag{31}
$$

*Equation 32, Bespoke Sensitivity of the 120 Degree Ceiling.*
The corners of a grid of uncured glass transitions and curvature parameters that the article assumes representative move the 120 degree ceiling between 0.741 and 0.899.

$$
\alpha_{\text{vit}} = \frac{120/180}{0.7 + 0.3 \times 120/180} \approx 0.741,
\qquad
\alpha_{\text{vit}} = \frac{160/220}{0.3 + 0.7 \times 160/220} \approx 0.899
\tag{32}
$$

**Equation 33, Total Dwell of Two-Stage Cures Against the Autoclave.**
Adding the datasheet's post-cure to each low-temperature cure gives total dwells of three and eleven times the autoclave-only dwell.
[MTM45-1 Prepreg Technical Data Sheet, Cytec Industrial Materials][ref_mtm45_datasheet]

$$
\frac{t_{\text{init}} + t_{\text{post}}}{t_{\text{ac}}},
\qquad
\frac{4 + 2}{2} = 3,
\qquad
\frac{20 + 2}{2} = 11
\tag{33}
$$

**Equation 34, Wright Learning Curve.**
Recurring unit cost falls as a power of the cumulative unit number, with an exponent equal to the logarithm of the progress ratio over the logarithm of two.
[Experience Curve Effects][ref_learning_curve]
[Military Airframe Costs: The Effects of Advanced Materials and Manufacturing Processes][research_rand_airframe_costs]

$$
C_{i} = C_{1}\,i^{b}
\qquad\qquad
b = \frac{\ln \varrho}{\ln 2}
\tag{34}
$$

**Equation 35, Break-Even Production Run.**
The number of aircraft needed to repay a programme is its cost divided by the recurring saving per aircraft.

$$
n_{\text{break-even}} = \frac{C_{\text{programme}}}{\Delta C_{\text{per aircraft}}}
\tag{35}
$$

**Equation 36, Surface Area of a Fuselage Half-Shell.**
One fuselage half is half a cylinder, so its surface is half of pi times the diameter times the length.
[Advanced Composite Cargo Aircraft Proves Large Structure Practicality, CompositesWorld][ref_cw_acca]

$$
A_{\text{skin}} = \frac{\pi D L}{2}
\tag{36}
$$

*Equation 37, Bespoke Layup Rate Demanded by the Out-Life.*
The article requires every ply of a half-shell to be laid within one out-life window at a constant rate, which sets the sustained rate as plies times skin area over the out-life in working hours.

$$
\dot{A} = \frac{N\,A_{\text{skin}}}{t_{\text{out}}\,h_{\text{day}}}
\tag{37}
$$

*Equation 38, Bespoke Maximum Plies Within the Out-Life.*
Inverting the same single-window construction gives the most plies a shop of a given sustained rate can lay on the shell before the material is out of time.

$$
N_{\text{max}} = \frac{\dot{A}\,t_{\text{out}}\,h_{\text{day}}}{A_{\text{skin}}}
\tag{38}
$$

### Notation

- $E_{f}$, the facesheet modulus, with $t_{\text{face}}$ the facesheet thickness
- $h_{c}$, the core depth
- $t_{w}$, the vessel wall thickness
- $\sigma_{\text{allow}}$, the allowable wall stress
- $m_{\text{shell}}$, the shell mass of the vessel
- $p_{\text{amb}}$, the ambient pressure
- $p_{\text{gauge}}$, the autoclave gauge pressure
- $p_{\text{in}}$, the pressure inside the bag
- $\Delta p_{\text{bag}}$, the consolidation pressure under a vacuum bag, with $\Delta p_{\text{autoclave}}$ that in an autoclave
- $\lambda h$, the product of the lapse rate $\lambda$ and the geopotential altitude $h$
- $R_{\text{air}}$, the specific gas constant of air
- $\phi_{0}$, the initial void fraction, with $\phi_{1}$ the void fraction after compression
- $\gamma$, the surface tension of the uncured resin
- $r_{\text{min}}$, the smallest void radius that the consolidation pressure can close
- $k_{H}$, the Henry's law constant
- $k$, the permeability of the fibre bed
- $\mu$, the dynamic viscosity of the fluid
- $d_{f}$, the fibre diameter
- $V_{f}$, the fibre volume fraction
- $\kappa$, the Kozeny constant
- $\varphi$, the porosity of the channel network
- $t_{\text{sweep}}$, the time for a fluid to sweep the flow path
- $\alpha$, the degree of cure
- $H_{\text{ult}}$, the ultimate heat of reaction
- $E_{a}$, the activation energy
- $\alpha_{\text{th}}$, the through-thickness thermal diffusivity
- $\mathrm{Nu}$, the Nusselt number
- $h_{\text{autoclave}}$, the convective heat transfer coefficient in the autoclave, with $h_{\text{oven}}$ that in an oven
- $T_{g}$, the glass transition temperature
- $T_{g0}$, the glass transition temperature of the uncured resin, with $T_{g\infty}$ that of the fully cured resin
- $\lambda_{D}$, the DiBenedetto curvature parameter
- $\alpha_{\text{vit}}$, the degree of cure at vitrification
- $C_{i}$, the recurring cost of the $i$th unit, with $C_{1}$ that of the first
- $\varrho$, the progress ratio
- $n_{\text{break-even}}$, the number of aircraft needed to repay the programme
- $A_{\text{skin}}$, the skin area of one fuselage half-shell
- $\dot{A}$, the sustained layup rate
- $t_{\text{out}}$, the out-life of the prepreg in days
- $h_{\text{day}}$, the working hours a day
- $N_{\text{max}}$, the most plies that can be laid within the out-life
